sources.news_title: Flávio Bolsonaro Becomes a Florida Man
sources.text:
Flávio Bolsonaro Becomes a Florida Man
Just like his father, the far-right senator fled Brazil following his presidential election loss.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fallout of Brazil’s presidential election, a devastating train crash in Spain, and Russian efforts to court Africa.
Welcome to Miami
In 2022, then-Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro fled to the U.S. state of Florida after losing the presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Four years later, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has followed in his father’s footsteps.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fallout of Brazil’s presidential election, a devastating train crash in Spain, and Russian efforts to court Africa.
Welcome to Miami
In 2022, then-Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro fled to the U.S. state of Florida after losing the presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Four years later, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has followed in his father’s footsteps.
On Monday, Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Flávio to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports, just hours after the far-right senator lost the presidential election to Lula. Local authorities also reportedly alerted immigration officials to bar Flávio from leaving the country.
Flávio stands accused of corruption, tax evasion, and laundering more than $1 billion through an online gambling scheme. He is also separately under investigation for acquiring millions of dollars from Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced banker at the heart of one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals, to fund a biopic about his father, who was convicted of plotting an insurrection after his own 2022 presidential loss.
Flávio initially insisted that he planned to cooperate with Brazilian authorities. “I have never thought about leaving the country,” Flávio said on Monday. “I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
Yet according to Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration, the senator fled Brazil late Tuesday, using an Italian passport to enter Argentina by land before boarding a private flight to Ecuador and then another plane to the United States. He arrived in Miami early on Wednesday with his wife and two daughters after the Trump administration reportedly granted his family U.S. visas.
“I want to make it clear: I didn’t flee Brazil, I left for Brazil,” Flávio wrote in a statement on Tuesday, which he published on X, referring to himself as the “true elected president of Brazil.” He later deleted the statement and published a similar document calling himself “the leader of Brazil.” He thanked Argentine President Javier Milei and U.S. President Donald Trump for helping him escape, and he vowed to address the Brazilian people in the coming days to present a plan to oppose Lula.
Despite dozens of foreign leaders and the Organization of American States having recognized Lula’s surprise victory, Trump has questioned the results in a move largely seen as supporting Flávio’s electoral ambitions. “It looked like another rigged election, frankly,” Trump told reporters on Monday, without offering evidence.
Trump has a close relationship with the Bolsonaros, seeing them as far-right allies in the region. He has repeatedly clashed with Lula over trade policy, and he has parroted the Bolsonaro family’s allegations that Jair’s criminal conviction was a “witch hunt.” Leading up to last weekend’s election, Trump even held a photo op with Flávio, though the U.S. president stopped short of a formal endorsement.
The friendship has certainly been reciprocal. Flávio had promised to bolster ties with the United States if he won the presidency, vowing to join the Shield of the Americas anti-gang military program, establish a free trade agreement with Washington, and ally with the White House on critical mineral policy.
Those ties make Flávio’s decision to flee to Florida (Trump’s unofficial second base of operations) unsurprising. But what it means for the future of his political fortunes and those of the right-wing opposition that he leads is far less clear. “This feels like the ship has been left without a captain,” a Bolsonaro ally told CNN Brazil.
Today’s Most Read
- 5 Foreign-Policy Priorities for Democrats After the Midterms by FP Staff
- America’s Least Bad Option in Iran by Raphael S. Cohen and Howard J. Shatz
- Trump Has Lost the Foreign-Policy Debate by Jonathan Monten, Jordan Tama, and Josh Busby
What We’re Following
Deadly train crash. Spain suffered another train-related trauma on Wednesday, after the collision of two high-speed trains near the city of Toledo killed at least 68 people and injured around 100 others. Search-and-rescue operations are still underway.
The accident occurred early on Wednesday after an information technology failure involving railroad switching equipment stopped all trains on the heavily trafficked Madrid-Sevilla rail line. A train from Iryo, a competitor to the Spanish national rail line, stopped on the southbound tracks shortly after 8:30 a.m. local time. A few minutes later, the central control of Spanish rail gave the go-ahead for another southbound train from the state carrier RENFE to continue its journey through a roughly 15-mile stretch on the outskirts of Toledo, according to Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
The train is believed to have reached a speed of around 120 miles per hour when it slammed into the stalled Iryo train on the same track. “It was an accident that was truly inconceivable,” Puente said in a press conference.
The accident comes at a sensitive time for the Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who is facing a reelection fight in November. In January, a high-speed train derailment on the same line killed 46 people. And earlier this month, another high-speed train between Madrid and Barcelona caught fire, raising questions about the Spanish government’s oversight and maintenance of one of the world’s largest high-speed rail networks.—Keith Johnson
Putin courts Africa. This year’s two-day Russia-Africa summit kicked off in Moscow on Wednesday with a focus on bolstering the Kremlin’s reach on the continent. “The era when the destinies of entire continents were determined by a narrow bloc of states is coming to an irreversible end,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said, alluding to Moscow’s efforts to outbid China, Europe, and the United States for regional influence.
Putin emphasized Russia’s grain and fertilizer deliveries to more than 40 African countries; called for expanding Africa’s decision-making role in the U.S.-dominated World Bank and International Monetary Fund; and doubled down on Moscow’s security presence in the region, specifically with its paramilitary Wagner Group. Expanding ties with Africa could also help the Kremlin circumvent the impact of European sanctions.
Yet African nations may not be as enthused to strengthen ties with Moscow. Only around 22 African leaders attended this week’s summit, a significant drop from past years’ attendance. Some experts suspect that this is due to anger over Russia’s use of African soldiers in its war with Ukraine. “Security means little when young Nigerians are lured abroad and end up on a frontline they never chose,” Nigerian newspaper Vanguard wrote in an op-ed on Tuesday.
Britain’s budget proposal. British Finance Minister John Healey unveiled a highly anticipated 2027 budget plan on Wednesday that aims to help households weather surging energy bills and high fuel prices. The proposal is the first by Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government, which has made economic reform and fiscal discipline among the top items on its agenda.
According to Healey, the plan envisions giving around 20 million lower-valued homes a roughly $133 payment to help offset rising costs, extending a freeze on fuel duty rates until at least July, and abolishing standing gas bill charges for 23 million households. These energy-focused savings measures are in line with Burnham’s other efforts to provide Britons with price stability amid supply chain crises fueled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Among the budget’s other proposals, Healey vowed to reduce government borrowing from 4.2 percent of GDP this year to 3.4 percent of GDP next year, remove import duties on more than 100 products, increase the national minimum wage, and raise taxes on gambling and banks. This is a “budget for the worker, the sole trader, the parent at the school gate,” Healey said, adding that his proposal hopes to eliminate the current deficit and “get Britain’s finances into the black” within three years.
Critics, however, remain unimpressed with Healey’s promises, arguing that the timeline for relief could be slow and that energy shocks will likely still be felt by many Britons. The proposal also delayed addressing several major concerns, such as how exactly Healey will increase defense spending and continued public anger toward high taxes, until next year.
Odds and Ends
A Belgian chocolate competition is giving Willy Wonka a run for his money. Confectionary artisans from around the world gathered in Antwerp, Belgium, this week for a two-day chocolate sculpture contest. Participants of the World Chocolate Masters showcased several intricate creations, from a bird vase to an elf to an original video game character. But the winner of the event went to Italian chocolatier Tommaso Grollero, whose octopus sculpture earned him the highest overall score.
Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

sources.text:
Flávio Bolsonaro Flees Brazil, Arrives in Miami After Disputed Presidential Election
by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief
(Worthy News) – Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, arrived in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil through Argentina and Ecuador, defying a Supreme Court travel ban just days after losing a closely contested presidential election.
The 45-year-old senator crossed into Argentina late Tuesday with his wife and two daughters before boarding a private aircraft bound for Ecuador. The family subsequently flew to Miami, where they arrived Wednesday morning, according to The Wall Street Journal and Associated Press.
Bolsonaro’s departure followed a Brazilian Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports. He faces investigations involving alleged corruption and money laundering, accusations he denies. His supporters have accused Brazil’s judiciary of politically motivated persecution.
The political crisis erupted after leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff election with approximately 51.8% of the vote. Bolsonaro has refused to concede and challenged the results, alleging electoral irregularities.
President Donald Trump, a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, questioned the election’s legitimacy and supported allowing Flávio Bolsonaro and his family into the United States. The Trump administration approved visas for the family earlier this week.
The controversy echoes the experience of Jair Bolsonaro, who traveled to Florida after losing Brazil’s 2022 presidential election. The former president is now serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest following his conviction over an alleged attempt to overturn that election.
Flávio Bolsonaro’s arrival in the United States threatens to deepen diplomatic tensions between Washington and Brasília as Brazil confronts another bitter political confrontation over election results and judicial authority.

sources.news_title: Bolsonaro’s Flight to US Raises Stakes in Growing Trump-Lula Political Rift
sources.text:
Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday, Oct. 28, after leaving his country despite a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, raising the prospect of a new diplomatic confrontation between U.S. President Donald Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost Sunday’s presidential runoff to Lula but has refused to concede defeat. His departure comes amid criminal investigations in Brazil and growing scrutiny of the Trump administration’s involvement in the country’s political affairs.
According to Reuters, Bolsonaro and his family traveled through Argentina and Ecuador before reaching Florida aboard a private aircraft. Washington has confirmed that the family will receive U.S. entry visas.
The developments have transformed Brazil’s disputed political aftermath into an international controversy, with questions emerging about Washington’s support for the Bolsonaro family and the consequences for relations between the two countries.
Success
You are now signed up for our newsletter
Success
Check your email to complete sign up
Trump welcomes Bolsonaro as Lula condemns departure
Speaking to reporters early Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Trump expressed support for Bolsonaro’s arrival in the United States.
“Well, I would approve,” Trump said, according to Reuters.
“I think they’re fine people,” he added. “The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible.”
Trump also defended Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest following his conviction for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election.
The U.S. president has repeatedly characterized the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution as politically motivated, although he emphasized Wednesday that Brazil remains a sovereign country.
Lula, meanwhile, sharply criticized Flávio Bolsonaro’s departure, suggesting the senator should have remained in Brazil to answer the allegations against him.
“I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula said, according to an Associated Press report.
“This act of leaving Brazil is shameful,” he added.
Bolsonaro’s departure came after Brazilian authorities ordered him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports within 24 hours. The Supreme Court cited concerns that he might flee the country and his substantial financial resources.
His failure to comply resulted in the cancellation of those documents.
However, the Associated Press reported that Bolsonaro also possesses an Italian passport, which a Brazilian diplomatic source said he used to enter Argentina.
The United States subsequently confirmed plans to issue visas to Bolsonaro, his wife, and their two daughters. The type of visa granted has not been publicly established, and the decision does not necessarily constitute political asylum.
Washington’s involvement in Brazilian politics faces renewed scrutiny
The controversy follows revelations that senior U.S. State Department officials had reportedly pursued a strategy intended to return the Bolsonaro family to power.
In an Oct. 24 investigation, Reuters cited 10 current and former U.S. officials who described efforts by two Trump administration appointees, Darren Beattie and Ricardo Pita, to advance the family’s political interests.
According to the investigation, the officials initially sought to facilitate Jair Bolsonaro’s political return before shifting their attention to his son following the former president’s conviction.
The report also described efforts to impose sanctions on Brazilian officials, including Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who has overseen criminal proceedings involving members of the Bolsonaro family.
Washington previously accused Moraes of violating freedom of expression through restrictions on political speech and social media content. Moraes has defended his actions as necessary to combat disinformation and protect Brazil’s democratic institutions.
The State Department rejected suggestions that its actions were intended to improperly influence Brazil’s political system.
“The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections,” spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Reuters.
Former State Department official Orna Blum, who previously oversaw Brazilian affairs, offered a different assessment. She argued that using American diplomatic and economic pressure to influence another country’s judicial proceedings risks crossing the boundary between legitimate foreign policy and political intervention.
Reuters said it could not determine whether the officials had acted on direct instructions from Trump or Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The diplomatic tensions predate Bolsonaro’s departure.
In July, Lula accused Washington of attempting to interfere in Brazil’s election after his government denied visas to two American officials.
The U.S. State Department rejected those accusations, maintaining that the planned visit was routine.
Lula nevertheless emphasized that he wanted to avoid a direct confrontation with Washington.
“Trump sometimes seems to want to pick a fight with me,” Lula said, according to Reuters. “I don’t want a fight with him.”
Washington’s support for Bolsonaro now adds another complication to a relationship already strained by disputes over trade, judicial independence, and political sovereignty.
Political persecution or legitimate prosecution?
At the center of the controversy is a broader disagreement over whether Brazil’s judicial proceedings against the Bolsonaro family represent legitimate law enforcement or politically motivated persecution.
Flávio Bolsonaro faces investigations involving alleged corruption, money laundering, and financial irregularities.
According to the Associated Press, one investigation concerns allegations that a sports betting company was used to launder money obtained through fraudulent deductions from government pensions.
Another involves allegations that Bolsonaro accepted millions of dollars from a banker accused of financial misconduct.
Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing in both cases.
Before leaving Brazil, he publicly dismissed the court’s passport order as an intimidation tactic.
“I never thought about leaving the country,” Bolsonaro said in a video published Monday.
He also promised to surrender his passports and defend himself against the allegations, describing the judicial measures as an attempt to silence him.
His sudden departure surprised members of his own political organization.
“We are surprised by the news,” campaign manager and Senator Rogério Marinho told Reuters.
Marinho explained that campaign officials had been discussing how Bolsonaro could assume leadership of the opposition following an election in which he received nearly 60 million votes.
Bolsonaro’s supporters have also questioned the impartiality of Justice Moraes, whom they accuse of using judicial authority against political opponents.
However, the investigations remain ongoing, and allegations of political persecution do not establish that the criminal inquiries are unfounded.
Brazil’s electoral authorities reported that Lula won the presidential runoff with approximately 51.8 percent of the vote, defeating Bolsonaro by roughly 4.4 million votes.
Bolsonaro has challenged the election’s legitimacy, but no substantiated evidence has emerged demonstrating fraud sufficient to overturn the result. His Liberal Party has acknowledged Lula’s victory.
The senator’s departure also carries implications for his political future. His Senate term expires on Jan. 31, 2027, after which he will lose the special judicial jurisdiction associated with his position.

Meanwhile, the family’s presence in the United States creates a potential diplomatic dilemma.
Jair Bolsonaro similarly traveled to Florida following his 2022 election defeat, although he eventually returned to Brazil.
This time, however, Flávio Bolsonaro has left while facing active investigations and after failing to comply with a judicial order.
Whether he intends to seek political asylum, remain temporarily in the United States, or continue leading Brazil’s opposition from abroad remains uncertain.
For Washington and Brasília, the immediate question is whether the Trump administration’s willingness to receive Bolsonaro will further damage an already strained relationship, particularly if Brazilian authorities seek additional legal action against him.

sources.news_title: Defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after fleeing Brazil
Bolsonaro Lands in U.S. After Fleeing Brazil Following Defeat
What to know about Brazil's Bolsonaro's departure to the US after his electoral defeat
sources.text:
SAO PAULO (AP) — Flávio Bolsonaro fled with his family to Miami after his defeat by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil's presidential elections.
The 45-year-old ally of U.S President Donald Trump landed in Florida on Wednesday, even after Brazil's Supreme Court labeled him a flight risk due to pending corruption investigations and ordered the seizure of his passports. The U.S. granted visas to Bolsonaro and his family this week.
Here's what to know about the election and Bolsonaro's departure:
Bolsonaro cried foul in the election
Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of the election on Oct. 4 by 2.2 million votes, but he lost the runoff on Sunday by double that amount of votes, as abstention rates and invalid votes dropped to historic lows.
Politicians say Lula could have won by more but voters were hampered by bus shortages in Sao Paulo and Salvador, where the president is popular.
Both candidates alleged voter suppression in their strongholds and called for an extension of voting hours beyond 5 p.m. Three minutes before polls were due to close, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin granted a two-hour extension.
Brazil's electoral court reported that some 35,000 people voted during that expanded window but that the extension did not affect the electoral outcome. More than 128 million people voted in total.
World leaders and organizations accepted the results
Bolsonaro said he would seek to have the election results annulled, but took no action before he fled.
His own Liberal Party elected six governors, 121 lawmakers and 19 senators in the most recent elections, and accepted all the results Monday evening, including his loss.
“We acknowledge the presidential election result as proclaimed by the superior electoral court,” the Liberal Party said in a statement.
The Carter Center and the Organization of American States sent election observers to Brazil. Neither found irregularities.
Political leaders from around the world congratulated Lula on his win. Notable exceptions included Bolsonaro allies Trump, who said Brazil’s election was “rigged,” and Argentina’s President Javier Milei, who did not comment.
Even Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella, a right-wing Bolsonaro ally, congratulated the 81-year-old Lula, whose term begins Jan. 5.
“In the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Iván Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won,” De La Espriella said on X. “Neither Lula decides for the Colombians, nor do I decide for the Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE!”
The electronic voting system in Brazil has rarely been challenged in a meaningful way. Bolsonaro's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, claimed — without evidence — there had been electoral fraud in the 2022 presidential election. He subsequently headed an unsuccessful attempt to overthrow Lula, his successor.
Investigations are pending against Bolsonaro
Minutes after the presidential election results were announced, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the seizure of Flávio Bolsonaro's passports.
The senator is under Supreme Court investigation for the financing of a movie about his father’s life, “Dark Horse,” including more than $12 million from a disgraced former banker, Daniel Vorcaro. He is also accused of laundering money and fraudulent use of money intended for senior citizens.
A Brazilian diplomat who was not authorized to speak about the matter publicly told The Associated Press that Bolsonaro used an Italian passport to enter Argentina and — despite considering him a flight risk — Brazil’s federal police were not monitoring him and his family before they fled to Florida.
The same Supreme Court justice led an investigation into Jair Bolsonaro's coup attempt that resulted in the former president being sentenced to 27 years under house arrest.

sources.news_title: Flavio Bolsonaro's Arrival in the U.S. After Escaping Lula's Regime Threats
sources.text:
On October 28, Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his wife and two daughters, landed at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport after a hasty exit from Brazil driven by fears for their safety. This move follows a highly questionable election in which leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva triumphed.
The Bolsonaro family crossed into Argentina before boarding a private jet to Miami. Reports indicate they entered Argentina just before midnight on October 27, using legitimate travel papers. After a brief stop in Ecuador, they reached Miami early on the 28th.
Following missed deadlines imposed by Brazil’s Supreme Court, Bolsonaro had his passports revoked amidst a money-laundering inquiry, which he firmly asserts he did not participate in. The family received assistance from the U.S. State Department for their visas, and President Donald Trump welcomed them, describing them as “fine people.”
Footage captured their arrival, showing the senator with a subdued demeanor as he stepped off the plane wearing a navy polo and backpack. His family followed closely behind, all of them shielding themselves from the media under umbrellas.
POLL: Should Trump Cut Off Aid To Countries That Side With Iran Over America?
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family have landed in Miami after fleeing his country.
This comes a day after they were granted United States visas by the Trump administration. pic.twitter.com/oB91ejWab5
— The Associated Press (@AP) October 28, 2026
Bolsonaro’s leave comes on the heels of a contentious election outcome that many view as suspicious due to late voting extensions mandated by a court linked to Lula’s administration. Critics deem this as contributing to the ongoing political turmoil.
President Trump commented on the election, stating it appeared “rigged” and quite odd, though he opted not to endorse a candidate outright.
With Flavio fleeing to the U.S., concerns loom over potential legal actions from Lula’s government against him and related political figures, including his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was imprisoned in 2025.
The Lula administration has labeled objections to the election results as a “coup attempt,” targeting Bolsonaro and his supporters severely. Legal proceedings have ensnared numerous opposition members and activists, prompting accusations of political targeting by the current government.
The U.S. government has introduced sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes, further highlighting the intensifying tensions and political repression against dissenting voices in Brazil.

sources.news_title: Bolsonaro’s son and family flee to Miami after refusing to concede
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami
sources.text:
Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami, declares himself rightful leader of Brazil
The senator said without providing evidence that he was a victim of an electoral coup d’etat by leftist leader Lula and the Supreme Court
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who arrived in the US on Wednesday, has declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil, alleging an electoral coup d’etat had been carried out by the country’s Supreme Court and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won the presidential election by over 4 million votes.
Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s election and left Brazil for Miami, where he and his family received US visas, thanked Argentine leader Javier Milei and US President Donald Trump for helping him leave his country and for welcoming him.
In an initial open letter posted on social media, Bolsonaro declared himself “the elected president”. He then deleted that version, and updated with another letter in which he said he was the rightful “leader” of Brazil.

sources.news_title: Bolsonaro’s midnight escape: Defeated candidate flees Brazil, Lula calls it ‘shameful’
sources.text:
In a dramatic getaway that reads more like a political thriller than a concession speech, defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro bolted the country Tuesday night with his wife and two daughters, crossing into Argentina by land, then boarding a private jet for Ecuador and eventually Miami. The 45-year-old senator lost Sunday’s runoff election to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%, but rather than comply with a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports amid money-laundering investigations, he simply vanished.
Now on U.S. soil, Bolsonaro’s flight has sparked fury from Lula, who accused the Bolsonaro family of treating Brazil like a second homeland and suggested the senator has something to hide. The Trump administration has granted visas to Bolsonaro and his family.
Lula did not mince words Tuesday, calling the candidate’s escape shameful. At an event marking his 81st birthday in Brasília, Lula took aim at the whole clan, according to a translation by the Guardian: “Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing.”
In remarks reported by CNN Brasil, Lula questioned what weighs on a person’s conscience after losing an election and fleeing his own country. “If you have nothing to hide, then you have nothing to fear,” he said. “Someone who secretly leaves the country surely has something to hide.”
The Brazilian Supreme Court had ordered Flávio Bolsonaro to turn in his passports, diplomatic as well as regular, by midday Tuesday as part of a money-laundering probe. He has denied the allegations, saying after receiving the order that he would defend himself against what he called a “travesty” and a clear attempt at intimidation. He never handed them over, and federal police have since canceled them, CNN Brasil reported, though allies say he also holds an Italian passport. But by Tuesday night, he was already across the border.
The senator and his family slipped into Argentina via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a key crossing into the province of Misiones, at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. Argentina’s migration authority said the family carried valid documents and had no legal barriers to entry. Forty minutes later, they boarded a private jet operated by Baires Fly S.A., which took off for Guayaquil, Ecuador, shortly after midnight. Flight data shows the plane reached Guayaquil around 4 a.m. Wednesday before quickly heading on to Miami’s Opa-locka Executive Airport.
The timing of the escape remains murky. Allies last saw Bolsonaro around 6 p.m. Monday, roughly 29 hours before he turned up at the Argentine border. Nobody seems to know where he spent that time or how he covered the roughly 19-hour road trip from Brasília without detection. Critics are now asking how Brazil’s federal police let him slip away.
President Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling Bolsonaro and his family “fine people.” Talking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on his way back from a Texas campaign swing, Trump described the Brazilian election as really strange and terrible, though he said he took no side. A senior U.S. State Department official confirmed visas would be issued to Bolsonaro and his family.
The episode threatens to widen the gulf between the hemisphere’s two most populous nations. Lula has charged that Washington is in cahoots with the Bolsonaros to restore the family to power—a charge amplified by Reuters reporting on a U.S. State Department campaign to bring the Bolsonaros back into office ahead of Sunday’s vote. Some in Lula’s government also suspect the senator’s allies spent Tuesday planting word that he was already headed to the U.S., to throw everyone off his real route through Argentina.
Close ally Paulo Figueiredo says Bolsonaro will hold a press conference Thursday in Miami, where he will presumably explain why a candidate who said he had “never thought about leaving the country” suddenly flew halfway across the hemisphere under cover of night. According to a Trump adviser who spoke to CNN, administration officials knew Monday that Bolsonaro faced a 24-hour passport deadline and let him know America’s door was open. Americans might have a question of their own: why is Washington picking favorites in another country’s election, then rolling out the welcome mat when its candidate loses?
